In this study, the integration of a two-dimensional van der Waals material (Fe GaTe ) with an organic polymer (P(VDF-TrFE)) addresses challenges associated with lattice matching, as illustrated in Figure R2. The strong interfacial coupling observed in our device, encompassing both the upper P(VDF-TrFE)/ Fe GaTe and bottom Fe GaTe /P(VDF-TrFE) interfaces, is characteristic of organic-inorganic van der Waals heterostructures. Interface formation in such systems relies primarily on physical adsorption and intermolecular forces, circumventing the need for stringent chemical bonding or precise lattice alignment (Chem. Rev. 2025, 125, 445-520). Furthermore, the incorporation of organic molecules or polymers during the synthesis of two-dimensional materials allows for flexible control of interlayer spacing, effectively accommodating the size of the organic components and mitigating lattice mismatch (Chem. Mater. 2023, 35, 10295-10315; Chem. Soc. Rev. 2020, 49, 6866-6883). Our device fabrication process, involving spin-coating a P(VDF-TrFE) solution onto the Fe GaTe surface followed by annealing, leverages the ability to form large-area periodic structures through solvent control or twisted stacking. These periodicities, exceeding atomic lattice scales, further alleviate constraints imposed by atomic-level lattice matching (Nat. Chem. 2025). The non-crystalline nature of the organic-inorganic interface also facilitates the reduction of dislocation density through the formation of superlattices (Chem. Soc. Rev. 2020, 49, 6866-6883). Finally, the inherent flexibility of the ferroelectric polymer (PVDF-TrFE) chains allows for interfacial deformation, enabling adaptation to the rigid crystal lattice of the inorganic layer via localized bending or segmental reorganization (Chem. Rev. 2025 125, 445-520; Nat. Chem. 2025, 16, 201-209). Figure R2 a, TEM image of the interface between the upper layer P(VDF-TrFE) and Fe GaTe . b, TEM image of the interface between Fe GaTe and the bottom layer P(VDF-TrFE). Comment 2. The author attributes the modulation of Fe2GaTe2 magnetism to strain transferred via the inverse piezoelectric effect of P(VDF-TrFE). How do the authors distinguish charge-mediated mechanisms, such as electrostatic doping or interfacial electric field effects, as dominant factors? Response 2: We extend our sincere gratitude to the reviewers for their insightful suggestions. The primary innovation of this study lies in the manipulation of the Fe GaTe lattice structure via strain engineering, accomplished through the polarization of P(VDF-TrFE). Leveraging the significant piezoelectric and ferroelectric characteristics of P(VDF-TrFE) films, both the induced strain and ferroelectric polarization resulting from gate-voltage application have the potential to influence the electronic properties of Fe GaTe . To disentangle the contributions of these two mechanisms, we fabricated both top-gate and bottom-gate device architectures. In the bottom-gate configuration, P(VDF-TrFE) induces both pronounced strain modulation and ferroelectric polarization modulation under gate voltage. Conversely, in the top-gate configuration, the presence of interfacial shear hysteresis arising from the rigid substrate significantly diminishes device deformation, thereby substantially attenuating stress transfer to the Fe GaTe layer. Consequently, ferroelectric polarization modulation becomes the dominant effect in this configuration, rendering the strain effect negligible. Through a systematic comparison of the performance characteristics of Fe GaTe devices employing both top-gate and bottom-gate configurations, we have effectively achieved a separation of the strain modulation and ferroelectric modulation mechanisms. Figure R3 a, Schematic diagram of polarization strain control and ferroelectric control of the bottom layer P(VDF-TrFE) in a device. b, Schematic diagram of ferroelectric control of the polarization of the top layer P(VDF-TrFE) in a device. The primary mechanism by which the P(VDF-TrFE) layer influences Fe GaTe is through ferroelectric polarization control, with minimal contribution from strain effects. Application of an electric field to reverse the ferroelectric polarization generates bound charges within the P(VDF-TrFE) layer. These charges, through short-range Coulombic interactions, induce a redistribution of charge carriers at the Fe GaTe interface. This charge transfer directly modulates the Fermi level position within Fe GaTe , thereby affecting its electronic filling state. This interfacial charge transfer, a well-established mechanism in multiferroic heterostructures, facilitates magnetoelectric coupling whereby alterations in carrier concentration controlled by ferroelectric polarization reconfigure the magnetic properties, enabling non-volatile magnetic switching (ACS Nano 2018, 12, 9558-9567; Nano Lett. 2024, 24, 5929-5936; Adv. Mater. 2025, 2500534; Appl. Phys. Lett. 2025, 126, 122901). The strain imparted by the P(VDF-TrFE) layer is substantially constrained by the rigid substrate, leading to interfacial shear stress. Consequently, the strain gradient decays sharply with increasing distance from the interface, resulting in minimal mechanical strain being transmitted to the Fe GaTe layer. This strain is demonstrably below the threshold required to induce lattice changes (Figure R4, Raman and XRD measurements of the polarized P(VDF-TrFE) layer confirm the structural integrity of the Fe GaTe lattice). As depicted in Figure 1e, while the P(VDF-TrFE) layer modulates the anomalous Hall resistance and coercive field of the Fe GaTe device under varying voltage polarization conditions, the direction of the easy magnetization axis remains invariant. Figure R4 a, XRD change curve of the upper layer P(VDF-TrFE) polarized device. The inset shows the Fe GaTe a axis and c axis as a function of polarization voltage. b, Raman change curve of the upper layer P(VDF-TrFE) polarized device. In the bottom-gate configuration, the polarization of the P(VDF-TrFE) layer simultaneously induces ferroelectric modulation and piezoelectric strain effects within the Fe GaTe thin film. Raman spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction analyses performed under varying polarization voltages reveal discernible alterations in the Fe GaTe lattice structure, as evidenced by shifts in characteristic Raman peaks and systematic changes in the a/c lattice constant ratio (Fig. 2d-2e). These observations indicate effective strain transfer from the P(VDF-TrFE) layer to the Fe GaTe lattice, leading to lattice distortion and a subsequent redistribution of its magnetic anisotropy. First-principles calculations (Figure 2f) provide theoretical corroboration of the correlation between strain and changes in magnetic anisotropy, lending further support to the experimental findings. Figure 2 d, Raman spectra of the dual-gate device as a function of the bottom layer polarization voltage, V , and the Raman spectra were measured at 300 K. The Raman spectra of the dual-gate device are shown in the figure below. The insets show the variation of the A peak of Fe GaTe and the position of the β peak of P(VDF-TrFE) with the polarization voltage V , as well as the error bars for five devices measured under the same conditions. e, XRD image of a device obtained at zero bias, the inset shows the variation of the in-plane lattice constant a and the out-of-plane lattice constant c with the bottom polarization voltage V . f, Variation of Fe GaTe magnetic anisotropy with strain calculated from first principles, the inset shows a schematic diagram of the variation of the magnetic moment orientation of the Fe sites within Fe GaTe . To ascertain the efficacy of strain transfer from the P(VDF-TrFE) ferroelectric polymer to the Fe GaTe lattice, we employed Raman spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to characterize the heterostructure device. As depicted in Figure 2d, application of varying polarization voltages to the underlying P(VDF-TrFE) layer resulted in a significant shift in the A Raman characteristic peak position of Fe GaTe . This peak position shift exhibited a linear relationship with the magnitude and direction of the polarization voltage, indicating controllable deformation of the Fe GaTe lattice structure. The systematic shift in Raman peak positions directly reflects alterations in interatomic bonding states or bond lengths, serving as a sensitive indicator of lattice strain or deformation. Complementary XRD results, presented in Figure 2e, demonstrate that the application of different polarization voltages systematically modulated the lattice constants a and c of Fe GaTe . Given that lattice constants (a, c) are fundamental parameters defining a crystal structure, their observed changes provide direct evidence of overall lattice deformation, encompassing in-plane compression/tension and out-of-plane expansion/contraction. These findings further substantiate the effective transfer of strain from P(VDF-TrFE), leading to a measurable alteration of the intrinsic lattice structure of Fe GaTe . In our multi-device logic array demonstrations, the variability observed in coercivity, Hall resistance, and switching voltage across devices is primarily attributable to inherent process-related factors. These include: (1) thickness variations (±10%) and domain structure inhomogeneities arising from the mechanical exfoliation of the Fe GaTe ferromagnetic layer; and (2) deviations in the spin-coated P(VDF-TrFE) ferroelectric polymer film thickness (<±5 nm), variations in the distribution of crystalline phases (with the β phase constituting 70-85%), and differences in domain size (50-200 nm), collectively leading to fluctuations in the electric field coupling efficiency. Through optimization of process parameters, we have successfully developed a comprehensive fabrication scheme, enabling us to constrain the variability in intrinsic device performance parameters, such as coercive field, Hall resistance, and switching voltage, to within a fluctuation range of 5-10%. Comment 5. The author suggests, unlike conventional heterostructure devices suffering from lattice mismatch-induced interfacial defects, the van der Waals interface offers enhanced thermal stability. Have the authors quantitatively evaluated how device performance (e.g., AHE, coercivity, strain sensitivity) changes with temperature, particularly across the ferroelectric Curie temperature or near the upper limits of operational range? Response 5: We appreciate the reviewers' insightful feedback. While all demonstrations in the main text were conducted at room temperature, we have included a temperature-dependent characterization of device performance in the supplementary information. Specifically, the polarization control characteristics were investigated within a temperature range of 280 K to 380 K. Figure R6a displays the device's resistance-temperature characteristics under an in-plane magnetic field (θ = 0°). As temperature increases from 280 K to 380 K, both the anomalous Hall resistance (R ) and coercive field (H ) exhibit a monotonic decrease, eventually vanishing above the Curie temperature (T ≈ 327 K) of Fe GaTe . This behavior stems from the ferromagnetic-to-paramagnetic phase transition in Fe GaTe at T , where the spontaneous magnetization strength and long-range ferromagnetic order are disrupted. Since the anomalous Hall effect is fundamentally a topological transport phenomenon induced by ferromagnetic order, its presence is contingent on a non-zero spontaneous magnetization and the associated band structure within the ferromagnetic material. Consequently, the anomalous Hall effect disappears in the paramagnetic phase. Upon applying a -10 V bottom gate voltage to control ferroelectric polarization, significant changes are observed in the anomalous Hall resistance, coercive field, and easy axis of magnetization. During the temperature ramp from 280 K to 380 K, both the anomalous Hall resistance and coercive field initially decrease. Notably, the anomalous Hall effect, which had previously vanished, reappears at approximately 340 K. This reappearance arises from ferroelectric-ferromagnetic coupling induced by the bottom-gate polarization. Polarized charges within the P(VDF-TrFE) ferroelectric layer modulate the carrier concentration in Fe GaTe , enhancing exchange interactions in the ferromagnetic layer through interfacial charge transfer, thus effectively increasing the Curie temperature of Fe GaTe above 340 K. Correspondingly, a marked jump in the coercive field is observed near 340 K. As the temperature further increases from 280 K to 380 K, the ferroelectricity of P(VDF-TrFE) (70:30) gradually diminishes due to enhanced thermal fluctuations. This decay is attributed to intensified thermal motion of molecular chains, leading to a reduction in the ordering of ferroelectric dipoles. As the temperature approaches its Curie temperature (T ≈ 380 K), the thermal fluctuation energy becomes comparable to the ferroelectric domain stability energy barrier, initiating the formation of polar nanodomains. Above 380 K, the dipole moments become disordered. This ferroelectric decay directly weakens the regulatory effect, manifesting in two ways: (1) the difference between the polarized and initial states for R and H gradually converges as temperature increases (as indicated by the decreasing area of the blue region in Figure R6c-6d); and (2) the orientation of the easy axis of magnetization gradually returns to 90°. These observations confirm the temperature sensitivity of the ferroelectric layer's ability to control magnetic parameters. Response 1: We sincerely appreciate the reviewers' insightful and valuable comments, which have been crucial in refining the quality of our manuscript. Response 2: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their valuable comments. While the Langmuir-Blodgett (LB) technique offers a robust platform for fundamental research, enabling the fabrication of highly ordered model films, its inherent complexity, slow processing speed, elevated cost, and challenges in scalability limit its viability for the production of most practical devices. Conversely, although spin coating presents limitations regarding crystallinity and chain orientation control, these are counterbalanced by its considerable advantages in simplicity, speed, cost-effectiveness, scalability, adaptability to diverse substrates, and a practical range of achievable film thicknesses. Furthermore, extensive research has focused on spin-coated P(VDF-TrFE) ferroelectric thin films, yielding significant advancements in crystallinity and overall ferroelectric performance(Nature 2004, 428, 299-303 (2004); Science 2019, 364, 166-169; Small 2025, 21, 2502767; Adv. Funct. Mater. 2025, 35, 2412507; Polymers 2019, 11, 1096; Mat Sci Semicon Proc 2025, 196, 1109653; J Mater Sci 2020, 55:6696-6707). Following spin coating, the P(VDF-TrFE) film underwent a two-stage thermal treatment to enhance its ferroelectric properties. Initially, the film was dried at 70°C for 1 hour to facilitate solvent removal. Subsequently, it was annealed and crystallized at 130°C under vacuum(Nano Energy 2017, 32, 255-262; ACS Nano 2022, 16, 18355-18365; Polymer 2004, 45, 1679-1688; Polym Polym Compos 2016, 24, 167-172; Adv. Mater. Technol. 2025, e01513; J Mater Sci-mater El 2017, 28, 8391-8396). This process significantly improved the ferroelectricity of P(VDF-TrFE) through distinct mechanisms. The initial drying step at 70°C effectively removed residual solvents, mitigating defect formation during subsequent crystallization and preventing interference with the ordered alignment of molecular chains. Furthermore, vacuum annealing at 130°C, exceeding the material's Curie temperature, promoted enhanced molecular chain mobility, rearrangement, and growth. This resulted in the formation of larger, purer ferroelectric β-phase crystals characterized by a fully trans conformation. The vacuum environment also served to prevent high-temperature oxidative degradation. These crucial points have prompted us to conduct a more in-depth mechanical analysis of the device's operating mechanism. While we acknowledge that symmetrical shear constraints on the upper and lower polymer layers are ideal in a perfectly symmetrical suspended structure, the practical fabrication of devices introduces a critical asymmetry in mechanical boundary conditions. Specifically, the presence of the silicon substrate creates a fundamental disparity in strain transfer efficiency between the upper and lower polymer layers. Analogous to piezoelectric actuators, when P(VDF-TrFE) is situated on a silicon substrate, the strain generated through the inverse piezoelectric effect experiences significantly greater mechanical constraints during downward transmission due to the substrate's rigidity. These constraints are substantially more pronounced than those encountered during upward transmission. As a consequence, the strain transmission efficiency in the downward direction is demonstrably lower than that in the upward direction. Piezoelectric actuators have garnered significant attention as promising microactuators owing to their ease of fabrication, rapid response times, and compact form factors, leading to their widespread application in areas such as soft robotics, artificial muscles, and electronic devices. Among piezoelectric polymers, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) and its copolymers are particularly prevalent in the development of piezoelectric actuators. This is attributable to their lightweight nature, facile processing, high flexibility, and, crucially, the presence of the polar β-phase, which endows them with piezoelectric properties by facilitating dipole alignment in a unified direction(Chem. Rev. 2009, 109, 6632-6686; J. Intell. Mater. Syst. Struct. 2018, 29 2096−2104; Phys. Rev. Lett. 2007, 99, 047801). As illustrated in Figure R2, the actuator comprises a central carbon fiber layer serving as a rigid substrate, with polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) piezoelectric layers fabricated on either end. Deformation is achieved through the inverse piezoelectric effect of the PVDF material; the application of voltage to the PVDF layers induces axial strain (expansion or contraction). Given the actuator's multilayer composite structure (e.g., a symmetrical PVDF-carbon fiber-PVDF laminate), the central carbon fiber layer functions as a rigid substrate, thereby constraining deformation in proximity to the neutral axis. Consequently, stress propagation is impeded near the substrate interface, necessitating its transfer to the opposing end. This generates an asymmetric strain distribution across the upper and lower surfaces of the PVDF layers. Under voltage excitation, one surface of the PVDF layer elongates while the other contracts.
