### Reviewer 2

The manuscript by Cai et al. reports that development of multiferroic vdW heterostructures by integrating two-dimensional ferromagnetic Fe3GaTe2 with ferroelectric P(VDF-TrFE). The coupling between ferroelectric polarization and strain enables tunable modification of magnetic properties. The scope of this work aligns well the aim of Nature Communications, and is expected to attract broad interest across materials science and logic in memory community. Therefore, I would recommend publication in Nature Communications, after the authors addressing some comments listed below. 1. The author claims that atomically sharp interface of P(VDF-TrFE) and Fe3GaTe2 interface reduces interfacial scattering. Can the authors provide experimental evidence to prove high-quality, atomically sharp nature of the interface? 2. The author attributes the modulation of Fe2GaTe2 magnetism to strain transferred via the inverse piezoelectric effect of P(VDF-TrFE). How do the authors distinguish charge-mediated mechanisms, such as electrostatic doping or interfacial electric field effects, as dominant factors? 3. P(VDF-TrFE) is a soft polymer. How did the author confirm efficient mechanical strain transfer to the Fe3GaTe2 layer through vdW interface? Can the author provide any experimental evidence of this? 4. In the multi-device logic array demonstrations (AND/NAND/NOT/half-adder), what is the device-to-device variability in coercivity, Hall resistance, or switching voltage? How reproducible are the operations across cycles or fabrication batches? 5. The author suggests, unlike conventional heterostructure devices suffering from lattice mismatch-induced interfacial defects, the van der Waals interface offers enhanced thermal stability. Have the authors quantitatively evaluated how device performance (e.g., AHE, coercivity, strain sensitivity) changes with temperature, particularly across the ferroelectric Curie temperature or near the upper limits of operational range?

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript reports a dual-gated Fe₃GaTe₂/P(VDF-TrFE) heterostructure with voltage-controlled modulation of magnetic properties and demonstration of spin-based logic functionality. While the subject falls within the general interest of multiferroic 2D devices, I have serious concerns regarding the novelty of the work, the clarity of the physical mechanisms involved, and the scientific rigor of the data interpretation. Based on the issues outlined below, I do not recommend publication of the manuscript. Below are my detailed comments: 1. This manuscript lacks novelty. The magnetic properties of Fe3GaTe2, such as perpendicular magnetic anisotropy and the anomalous Hall effect, have already been thoroughly investigated (for example doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-32605-5). There is no need to revisit these aspects without offering new understanding. Moreover, the use of PVDF gating to modulate the magnetism of Fe3GaTe2 has already been explored in previous publications by the authors and their collaborators (doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-62159-1). In this manuscript, the only potentially novel aspect is the use of a dual-gate configuration. However, this part is not clearly explained in the manuscript, and the physical mechanism behind it is not convincingly discussed. I find this unsatisfactory. The authors should reorganize the manuscript, remove results that are already known or unrelated, and focus on articulating the genuinely new contribution of this work. Only after establishing the novelty and underlying physics should the logic gate demonstrations be presented as outcomes of the new device structure. 2. The PVDF layers used in the device are spin-coated, which typically leads to lower crystallinity and weaker chain alignment compared to more controlled methods such as Langmuir-Blodgett techniques. However, the manuscript does not mention any post-deposition annealing or provide structural characterization data such as AFM or XRD. Given that the claimed device functionality relies heavily on the ferroelectric and piezoelectric properties of PVDF, the authors should include direct evidence supporting its crystallinity, beta-phase content, and ferroelectricity either in the main text discussion or in the supplementary materials. Measurements such as P–E loops, PFM, or other relevant characterizations are necessary to validate these properties. Without such evidence, the fundamental basis for the proposed mechanism remains unconfirmed. Further, according to the device setting, the electric field on the PVDF is as large as 10MV/cm, we suggest the author check the P-E loops to confirm the integrity of the material. 3. The anisotropy constant Ku and the modeling shown in Fig. 1c are not accompanied by any explanation of the fitting or calculation method. Since similar results have already been reported in the literature, this part does not represent a novel contribution. I suggest moving these data to the Supplementary Material. However, if the authors choose to keep them in the main text, they should include a clear and quantitative description of how Ku is extracted. Without such explanation, the figure lacks reproducibility and interpretive value. 4. I have serious concerns about the discussion of the topological Hall effect (THE) in lines 178–195. Based on the experimental data provided, I do not see convincing evidence of THE. The characteristic non-monotonic features, such as a peak or dip in the Hall resistance, are not clearly present. The monotonic decrease after magnetic flipping is more likely due to spin canting rather than the emergence of a topological contribution. Despite this, the authors devote substantial space to speculating about THE without providing any supporting evidence such as magnetic imaging, for example as shown in DOI: 10.1002/adma.202403154. This weakens the clarity of the manuscript and risks misleading readers. Moreover, the citation of Ref. 26 (doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-32605-5) to support the presence of THE in Fe₃GaTe₂ is inappropriate, as this reference does not discuss THE in that system. I strongly recommend the authors revise this section thoroughly and reconsider the interpretation presented. 5. The authors propose that the bottom PVDF layer contributes both doping and strain, while the top PVDF layer contributes only doping. This asymmetry is used to explain the more pronounced effect of the bottom gate. However, the physical origin of this asymmetry is not clearly justified. It is unclear why the top PVDF layer would not also generate strain through the same inverse piezoelectric mechanism. The manuscript should provide a more detailed and mechanistic explanation for this asymmetry. 6. Moreover, I wonder whether the observed modulation is simply doping-driven rather than resulting from ferroelectric polarization. In the presented data, all responses to gate voltage, whether from the top or bottom PVDF layer, appear continuous and do not show any signature of abrupt switching or hysteresis that is typically associated with ferroelectric behavior. This could be because the applied gate voltages are much larger than the coercive voltage of PVDF, which may suppress the characteristic ferroelectric response. The authors should examine this carefully. Without such analysis, I have reason to suspect that similar modulation could be achieved using two non-ferroelectric dielectric layers, such as hBN and SiO2, through electrostatic doping alone. This possibility needs to be ruled out before drawing any conclusions about polarization-driven effects. 7. In lines 123–127, the authors cite Ref. 17 to support a mechanism involving C–F dipole coupling with Te lone pairs and spin-state reconfiguration of Fe atoms. However, Ref. 17 discusses PVDF/PAN/CNT composites and their bulk electrical conductivity, and is entirely unrelated to Fe3GaTe2 interfaces or d-orbital physics. This citation is inappropriate and misleading. The authors should replace or remove it and ensure that all references are directly relevant to the claims being made. 8. When building the spin logic devices, the author constructed the Fe3GaTe2/P(VDF-TrFE) bilayer rather than the discussed P(VDF-TrFE)/Fe3GaTe2/P(VDF-TrFE) trilayer system before, which causes inconsistency of the work. 9. How is Ref. 19 (DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-26271-2), a paper related to breast cancer, cited in this 2D materials paper? 10. Figure 1b is never referenced in the main text. It is possible that there is a typo or omission around line 163 where it was intended to be mentioned. 11. In the script, the author call \Theta_H=90 as perpendicular direction and \Theta_H=0 as in plane direction. This is contradictory to the fig. 1c inset.

Response 1: We appreciate the reviewers' insightful feedback and acknowledge their concerns regarding device quantity, reproducibility, and the current technological maturity of our approach. The paper focuses on innovative strategies and a novel prototype of an original device, rather than industrial manufacturing, aiming to address key scientific challenges such as high-power dissipation and the separation between storage and computation in the post-Moore era. It seeks to establish a foundation for groundbreaking advancements in compute-in-memory architectures that transcend the limitations of conventional von Neumann computing. Mechanical exfoliation was widely employed in two-dimensional material research for property exploration and proof-of-concept demonstrations of innovative strategies and novel device prototypes (Nature 2025, 641, 70-75; Nat. Electron. 2025, 8, 235-243; Nat. Mater. 2018, 17, 908-914; Nat. Synth. 2025, 4, 106-115). The central aim of this work is to introduce and validate a novel logic technology strategy predicated on the vertical stacking of two-dimensional van der Waals multiferroic heterostructures (e.g., Fe GaTe /P(VDF-TrFE)) to achieve ferroelectric-ferromagnetic coupling. Our primary objective is to explore, at a fundamental level, the potential for transcending the limitations inherent in CMOS technology. Previous research has proposed multiple low-power strategies based on mechanical exfoliation to address the limitations of CMOS technology, thereby laying the groundwork for the continued advancement of semiconductor devices. (Science 2019, 363, 6428; Nat. Electron. 2019, 2, 274-283; Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 1902; Adv. Mater. 2025, 37, 2413916; Adv. Funct. Mater. 2023, 33, 2212722). While scalable preparation techniques such as chemical vapor deposition (CVD) and molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) have been developed in the industry, the focus of this work lies in validating the feasibility of the device prototype. While our current prototypes rely on mechanical exfoliation, we contend that the scalability of this strategy is not fundamentally restricted. Wafer-level two-dimensional material CVD growth, large-area fabrication of ferroelectric polymers, and advanced van der Waals integration technologies have demonstrated viable routes toward scalable implementation. Previous studies have explored the feasibility of using chemical vapour deposition (CVD) technology to achieve large-area preparation of iron gallium telluride (Fe GaTe ). (Mater. Sci. 2025, arXiv:2505.06128). Addressing key scientific challenges related to large-scale production, such as material preparation and the development of novel integration strategies, will be the next step following this foundational study(Nat. Commun. 2025, 16, 3691; Nat. Commun. 2025, 16, 3448; Nat. Commun. 2025, 16, 7305). The resulting reconfigurable spin-in-logic devices demonstrate outstanding performance characteristics, including ultra-low single-operation energy consumption (0.5 aJ), nanosecond-level write speeds (5 ns), and highly stable logic gate arrays (AND/NAND/NOT) and half-adder circuits. This work has demonstrated innovative strategies and a novel prototype of an original device within spin-in-logic architectures that transcend the limitations of conventional von Neumann computing. Since magnetic fields are used to tune electrical resistance, this fact will be never used to implement digital devices because the presence of a magnet in an electronic circuit will make it bulky will the aim is to reduce the dimensions of any electronic circuit. Response 3: The operation mechanism of this device is based on electric field coupling, which is driven exclusively by an electric field rather than a magnetic field. Logical operations are entirely performed through electric pulses. By inducing polarization reversal in the P(VDF-TrFE) ferroelectric layer, the magnetic moment of Fe GaTe can be modulated via ferroelectric polarization and strain control, thereby tuning the device resistance (see Figures 3 and 4 in the main text). The external magnetic field is only required for initial setup—it serves solely to define the initial magnetization direction (analogous to the write field in MRAM) and is not applied during device operation. Modern magnetoelectronics and advancements in low-dimensional materials science have enabled significant progress in addressing the size limitations of traditional electromagnetic devices. In the proposed heterostructure, magnetism is inherent to the integrated two-dimensional ferromagnetic Fe GaTe layer, which is only a few to several dozen atomic layers (nanoscale) in thickness. This ultrathin magnetic layer functions as an integrated 'magnet,' vertically stacked within the nanoscale heterostructure alongside ferroelectric layers and electrodes, rather than existing as a discrete, macroscopic magnetic component. The magnetic field required for resistance control is generated by this integrated ultrathin ferromagnetic layer within the heterostructure, representing a highly localized phenomenon confined to the nanoscale region near the interface. Consequently, the entire device structure, including the magnetic components, can be fabricated at the micrometer scale or even smaller using advanced nanomanufacturing techniques. This van der Waals heterostructure strategy of vertically stacking two-dimensional materials effectively enhances functional density and integration per unit area, resulting in highly compact units containing magnetic layers. The successful commercialization of modern spin-electronic storage devices, such as STT-MRAM or SOT-MRAM based on magnetic tunnel junctions, integrated into CMOS processes at 22nm, 12nm, and more advanced nodes provides compelling evidence of this trend. The core of these storage units also incorporates nanoscale ferromagnetic layers (typically alloy films such as CoFeB, with thicknesses of only 1-2 nanometers), where the magnetic moment is switched using the torque generated by spin-polarized current, rather than an external magnetic field. This clearly demonstrates that magnetic functional components can be highly miniaturized and integrated akin to CMOS logic circuits, thereby meeting the stringent size requirements of modern digital chips. Therefore, the 'bulky' issue often associated with traditional magnetic components is not a primary concern in this context. Our strategy, based on two-dimensional multiferroic heterostructures, leverages magnetism as an intrinsic, nanoscale integrated functional layer with minimal thickness and spatial footprint, while efficiently utilizing space through a vertical stacking architecture. Combined with the ultimate goal of achieving electric field control via multiferroic coupling, this technological approach theoretically possesses the potential to realize high-density, miniaturized digital logic integration. This work is dedicated to exploring and validating the feasibility and unique advantages, such as non-volatility, of this novel integrated magnetoelectric device for logic functionalities. Response: We greatly appreciate the reviewer for the positive recommendation and valuable comments. We thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestions that are important for the improvement of the manuscript. We have addressed the reviewer’s suggestion in the following and in the revised manuscript. Comment 1. The author claims that atomically sharp interface of P(VDF-TrFE) and Fe3GaTe2 interface reduces interfacial scattering. Can the authors provide experimental evidence to prove high-quality, atomically sharp nature of the interface? Response 1: We are grateful to the reviewers for their insightful feedback. In this study, the integration of a two-dimensional van der Waals material (Fe GaTe ) with an organic polymer (P(VDF-TrFE)) addresses challenges associated with lattice matching, as illustrated in Figure R2. The strong interfacial coupling observed in our device, encompassing both the upper P(VDF-TrFE)/ Fe GaTe and bottom Fe GaTe /P(VDF-TrFE) interfaces, is characteristic of organic-inorganic van der Waals heterostructures. Interface formation in such systems relies primarily on physical adsorption and intermolecular forces, circumventing the need for stringent chemical bonding or precise lattice alignment (Chem. Rev. 2025, 125, 445-520). Furthermore, the incorporation of organic molecules or polymers during the synthesis of two-dimensional materials allows for flexible control of interlayer spacing, effectively accommodating the size of the organic components and mitigating lattice mismatch (Chem. Mater. 2023, 35, 10295-10315; Chem. Soc. Rev. 2020, 49, 6866-6883). Our device fabrication process, involving spin-coating a P(VDF-TrFE) solution onto the Fe GaTe surface followed by annealing, leverages the ability to form large-area periodic structures through solvent control or twisted stacking. These periodicities, exceeding atomic lattice scales, further alleviate constraints imposed by atomic-level lattice matching (Nat. Chem. 2025). The non-crystalline nature of the organic-inorganic interface also facilitates the reduction of dislocation density through the formation of superlattices (Chem. Soc. Rev. 2020, 49, 6866-6883). Finally, the inherent flexibility of the ferroelectric polymer (PVDF-TrFE) chains allows for interfacial deformation, enabling adaptation to the rigid crystal lattice of the inorganic layer via localized bending or segmental reorganization (Chem. Rev. 2025 125, 445-520; Nat. Chem. 2025, 16, 201-209). Figure R2 a, TEM image of the interface between the upper layer P(VDF-TrFE) and Fe GaTe . b, TEM image of the interface between Fe GaTe and the bottom layer P(VDF-TrFE). Comment 2. The author attributes the modulation of Fe2GaTe2 magnetism to strain transferred via the inverse piezoelectric effect of P(VDF-TrFE). How do the authors distinguish charge-mediated mechanisms, such as electrostatic doping or interfacial electric field effects, as dominant factors? Response 2: We extend our sincere gratitude to the reviewers for their insightful suggestions. The primary innovation of this study lies in the manipulation of the Fe GaTe lattice structure via strain engineering, accomplished through the polarization of P(VDF-TrFE). Leveraging the significant piezoelectric and ferroelectric characteristics of P(VDF-TrFE) films, both the induced strain and ferroelectric polarization resulting from gate-voltage application have the potential to influence the electronic properties of Fe GaTe . To disentangle the contributions of these two mechanisms, we fabricated both top-gate and bottom-gate device architectures. In the bottom-gate configuration, P(VDF-TrFE) induces both pronounced strain modulation and ferroelectric polarization modulation under gate voltage. Conversely, in the top-gate configuration, the presence of interfacial shear hysteresis arising from the rigid substrate significantly diminishes device deformation, thereby substantially attenuating stress transfer to the Fe GaTe layer. Consequently, ferroelectric polarization modulation becomes the dominant effect in this configuration, rendering the strain effect negligible. Through a systematic comparison of the performance characteristics of Fe GaTe devices employing both top-gate and bottom-gate configurations, we have effectively achieved a separation of the strain modulation and ferroelectric modulation mechanisms. Figure R3 a, Schematic diagram of polarization strain control and ferroelectric control of the bottom layer P(VDF-TrFE) in a device. b, Schematic diagram of ferroelectric control of the polarization of the top layer P(VDF-TrFE) in a device. The primary mechanism by which the P(VDF-TrFE) layer influences Fe GaTe is through ferroelectric polarization control, with minimal contribution from strain effects. Application of an electric field to reverse the ferroelectric polarization generates bound charges within the P(VDF-TrFE) layer. These charges, through short-range Coulombic interactions, induce a redistribution of charge carriers at the Fe GaTe interface. This charge transfer directly modulates the Fermi level position within Fe GaTe , thereby affecting its electronic filling state. This interfacial charge transfer, a well-established mechanism in multiferroic heterostructures, facilitates magnetoelectric coupling whereby alterations in carrier concentration controlled by ferroelectric polarization reconfigure the magnetic properties, enabling non-volatile magnetic switching (ACS Nano 2018, 12, 9558-9567; Nano Lett. 2024, 24, 5929-5936; Adv. Mater. 2025, 2500534; Appl. Phys. Lett. 2025, 126, 122901). The strain imparted by the P(VDF-TrFE) layer is substantially constrained by the rigid substrate, leading to interfacial shear stress. Consequently, the strain gradient decays sharply with increasing distance from the interface, resulting in minimal mechanical strain being transmitted to the Fe GaTe layer. This strain is demonstrably below the threshold required to induce lattice changes (Figure R4, Raman and XRD measurements of the polarized P(VDF-TrFE) layer confirm the structural integrity of the Fe GaTe lattice). As depicted in Figure 1e, while the P(VDF-TrFE) layer modulates the anomalous Hall resistance and coercive field of the Fe GaTe device under varying voltage polarization conditions, the direction of the easy magnetization axis remains invariant. Figure R4 a, XRD change curve of the upper layer P(VDF-TrFE) polarized device. The inset shows the Fe GaTe a axis and c axis as a function of polarization voltage. b, Raman change curve of the upper layer P(VDF-TrFE) polarized device. In the bottom-gate configuration, the polarization of the P(VDF-TrFE) layer simultaneously induces ferroelectric modulation and piezoelectric strain effects within the Fe GaTe thin film. Raman spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction analyses performed under varying polarization voltages reveal discernible alterations in the Fe GaTe lattice structure, as evidenced by shifts in characteristic Raman peaks and systematic changes in the a/c lattice constant ratio (Fig. 2d-2e). These observations indicate effective strain transfer from the P(VDF-TrFE) layer to the Fe GaTe lattice, leading to lattice distortion and a subsequent redistribution of its magnetic anisotropy. First-principles calculations (Figure 2f) provide theoretical corroboration of the correlation between strain and changes in magnetic anisotropy, lending further support to the experimental findings. Figure 2 d, Raman spectra of the dual-gate device as a function of the bottom layer polarization voltage, V , and the Raman spectra were measured at 300 K. The Raman spectra of the dual-gate device are shown in the figure below. The insets show the variation of the A peak of Fe GaTe and the position of the β peak of P(VDF-TrFE) with the polarization voltage V , as well as the error bars for five devices measured under the same conditions. e, XRD image of a device obtained at zero bias, the inset shows the variation of the in-plane lattice constant a and the out-of-plane lattice constant c with the bottom polarization voltage V . f, Variation of Fe GaTe magnetic anisotropy with strain calculated from first principles, the inset shows a schematic diagram of the variation of the magnetic moment orientation of the Fe sites within Fe GaTe . Comment 3. P(VDF-TrFE) is a soft polymer. How did the author confirm efficient mechanical strain transfer to the Fe3GaTe2 layer through vdW interface? Can the author provide any experimental evidence of this? Response 3: We are deeply appreciative of the reviewers' insightful feedback. To ascertain the efficacy of strain transfer from the P(VDF-TrFE) ferroelectric polymer to the Fe GaTe lattice, we employed Raman spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to characterize the heterostructure device. As depicted in Figure 2d, application of varying polarization voltages to the underlying P(VDF-TrFE) layer resulted in a significant shift in the A Raman characteristic peak position of Fe GaTe . This peak position shift exhibited a linear relationship with the magnitude and direction of the polarization voltage, indicating controllable deformation of the Fe GaTe lattice structure. The systematic shift in Raman peak positions directly reflects alterations in interatomic bonding states or bond lengths, serving as a sensitive indicator of lattice strain or deformation. Complementary XRD results, presented in Figure 2e, demonstrate that the application of different polarization voltages systematically modulated the lattice constants a and c of Fe GaTe . Given that lattice constants (a, c) are fundamental parameters defining a crystal structure, their observed changes provide direct evidence of overall lattice deformation, encompassing in-plane compression/tension and out-of-plane expansion/contraction. These findings further substantiate the effective transfer of strain from P(VDF-TrFE), leading to a measurable alteration of the intrinsic lattice structure of Fe GaTe . Figure 2 d, Raman spectra of the dual-gate device as a function of the bottom layer polarization voltage, V , and the Raman spectra were measured at 300 K. The insets show the variation of the A peak of Fe GaTe and the position of the β peak of P(VDF-TrFE) with the polarization voltage V , as well as the error bars for five devices measured under the same conditions. Comment 4. In the multi-device logic array demonstrations (AND/NAND/NOT/half-adder), what is the device-to-device variability in coercivity, Hall resistance, or switching voltage? How reproducible are the operations across cycles or fabrication batches? Response 4: We gratefully acknowledge the reviewers' constructive feedback. In our multi-device logic array demonstrations, the variability observed in coercivity, Hall resistance, and switching voltage across devices is primarily attributable to inherent process-related factors. These include: (1) thickness variations (±10%) and domain structure inhomogeneities arising from the mechanical exfoliation of the Fe GaTe ferromagnetic layer; and (2) deviations in the spin-coated P(VDF-TrFE) ferroelectric polymer film thickness (<±5 nm), variations in the distribution of crystalline phases (with the β phase constituting 70-85%), and differences in domain size (50-200 nm), collectively leading to fluctuations in the electric field coupling efficiency. Through optimization of process parameters, we have successfully developed a comprehensive fabrication scheme, enabling us to constrain the variability in intrinsic device performance parameters, such as coercive field, Hall resistance, and switching voltage, to within a fluctuation range of 5-10%. As illustrated in the accompanying figure, the performance variability among 10 devices fabricated in different batches ranges from 3-6%. Comment 5. The author suggests, unlike conventional heterostructure devices suffering from lattice mismatch-induced interfacial defects, the van der Waals interface offers enhanced thermal stability. Have the authors quantitatively evaluated how device performance (e.g., AHE, coercivity, strain sensitivity) changes with temperature, particularly across the ferroelectric Curie temperature or near the upper limits of operational range? Response 5: We appreciate the reviewers' insightful feedback. While all demonstrations in the main text were conducted at room temperature, we have included a temperature-dependent characterization of device performance in the supplementary information. Specifically, the polarization control characteristics were investigated within a temperature range of 280 K to 380 K. Figure R6a displays the device's resistance-temperature characteristics under an in-plane magnetic field (θ = 0°). As temperature increases from 280 K to 380 K, both the anomalous Hall resistance (R ) and coercive field (H ) exhibit a monotonic decrease, eventually vanishing above the Curie temperature (T ≈ 327 K) of Fe GaTe . This behavior stems from the ferromagnetic-to-paramagnetic phase transition in Fe GaTe at T , where the spontaneous magnetization strength and long-range ferromagnetic order are disrupted. Since the anomalous Hall effect is fundamentally a topological transport phenomenon induced by ferromagnetic order, its presence is contingent on a non-zero spontaneous magnetization and the associated band structure within the ferromagnetic material. Consequently, the anomalous Hall effect disappears in the paramagnetic phase. Upon applying a -10 V bottom gate voltage to control ferroelectric polarization, significant changes are observed in the anomalous Hall resistance, coercive field, and easy axis of magnetization. During the temperature ramp from 280 K to 380 K, both the anomalous Hall resistance and coercive field initially decrease. Notably, the anomalous Hall effect, which had previously vanished, reappears at approximately 340 K. This reappearance arises from ferroelectric-ferromagnetic coupling induced by the bottom-gate polarization. Polarized charges within the P(VDF-TrFE) ferroelectric layer modulate the carrier concentration in Fe GaTe , enhancing exchange interactions in the ferromagnetic layer through interfacial charge transfer, thus effectively increasing the Curie temperature of Fe GaTe above 340 K. Correspondingly, a marked jump in the coercive field is observed near 340 K. As the temperature further increases from 280 K to 380 K, the ferroelectricity of P(VDF-TrFE) (70:30) gradually diminishes due to enhanced thermal fluctuations. This decay is attributed to intensified thermal motion of molecular chains, leading to a reduction in the ordering of ferroelectric dipoles. As the temperature approaches its Curie temperature (T ≈ 380 K), the thermal fluctuation energy becomes comparable to the ferroelectric domain stability energy barrier, initiating the formation of polar nanodomains. Above 380 K, the dipole moments become disordered. This ferroelectric decay directly weakens the regulatory effect, manifesting in two ways: (1) the difference between the polarized and initial states for R and H gradually converges as temperature increases (as indicated by the decreasing area of the blue region in Figure R6c-6d); and (2) the orientation of the easy axis of magnetization gradually returns to 90°. These observations confirm the temperature sensitivity of the ferroelectric layer's ability to control magnetic parameters. While the Langmuir-Blodgett (LB) technique offers a robust platform for fundamental research, enabling the fabrication of highly ordered model films, its inherent complexity, slow processing speed, elevated cost, and challenges in scalability limit its viability for the production of most practical devices. Conversely, although spin coating presents limitations regarding crystallinity and chain orientation control, these are counterbalanced by its considerable advantages in simplicity, speed, cost-effectiveness, scalability, adaptability to diverse substrates, and a practical range of achievable film thicknesses. Furthermore, extensive research has focused on spin-coated P(VDF-TrFE) ferroelectric thin films, yielding significant advancements in crystallinity and overall ferroelectric performance(Nature 2004, 428, 299-303 (2004); Science 2019, 364, 166-169; Small 2025, 21, 2502767; Adv. Following spin coating, the P(VDF-TrFE) film underwent a two-stage thermal treatment to enhance its ferroelectric properties. Initially, the film was dried at 70°C for 1 hour to facilitate solvent removal. Subsequently, it was annealed and crystallized at 130°C under vacuum(Nano Energy 2017, 32, 255-262; ACS Nano 2022, 16, 18355-18365; Polymer 2004, 45, 1679-1688; Polym Polym Compos 2016, 24, 167-172; Adv. Mater. Technol. 2025, e01513; J Mater Sci-mater El 2017, 28, 8391-8396). This process significantly improved the ferroelectricity of P(VDF-TrFE) through distinct mechanisms. The initial drying step at 70°C effectively removed residual solvents, mitigating defect formation during subsequent crystallization and preventing interference with the ordered alignment of molecular chains. Furthermore, vacuum annealing at 130°C, exceeding the material's Curie temperature, promoted enhanced molecular chain mobility, rearrangement, and growth. This resulted in the formation of larger, purer ferroelectric β-phase crystals characterized by a fully trans conformation. The vacuum environment also served to prevent high-temperature oxidative degradation. Collectively, these steps led to a significant enhancement in film crystallinity, β-phase content, and structural density, while simultaneously reducing grain boundaries and impurity defects. Consequently, spontaneous polarization strength was augmented, leakage current was diminished, and breakdown field strength was increased, culminating in optimized ferroelectric performance. In both poly(vinylidene fluoride-trifluoroethylene) [P(VDF-TrFE)] copolymers and polycrystalline PVDF thin films, a reduction in film thickness induces a significant size effect, primarily evidenced by grain refinement and a concomitant increase in domain wall density. This elevated domain wall density promotes a randomized distribution of local polarization orientations, thereby diminishing the cooperative polarization reversal between adjacent domains. Furthermore, decreasing the film thickness substantially amplifies the influence of interfacial effects on bulk polarization, macroscopically suppressing the characteristic discontinuous, non-linear polarization reversal process typically observed in ferroelectrics (Phys. Rev. Lett. 2018, 120, 26760). Analogous mechanisms are prevalent in other ferroelectric systems. For example, in PbTiO /SmScO 3 3 superlattices, the built-in electric field modulates polarization symmetry, and the interplay between elastic and electrostatic energies engenders macroscopically continuous piezoelectric responses despite the presence of microscopically discontinuous domains (Adv. Funct. Mater. 2025, e10402). Similarly, in BaTiO films with thicknesses ranging from 2 to 10 nm, nanoscale domains with 3 thicknesses as small as 0.4-0.8 nm (1-2 unit cells) have been observed. Specifically, the helical β phase of P(VDF-TrFE) is characterized by a high-density, ordered arrangement of C-F dipole moments. This characteristic arises from the polymer chains within the β phase adopting a fully trans (TTTT) conformation, where fluorine (F) and hydrogen (H) atoms are positioned on opposing sides of the carbon chain, thereby generating strong dipole moments perpendicular to the chain direction (Science 2021, 371, 1050-1056). The tellurium (Te) atoms on the Fe GaTe surface contribute 5p 3 2 orbital lone pair electrons, which interact with the C-F dipoles of P(VDF-TrFE) through electrostatic coupling. A comparable mechanism has been observed in BiFeO /P(VDF-TrFE) composite films, 3 where the lone pair electrons on the BiFeO surface couple with the C-F dipoles, creating a localized 3 electric field. This interfacial electric field, in turn, modulates the d electrons of Fe atoms in Fe GaTe through the orbital-spin correlation effect (Smart Mater. Struct. 2023, 32 045017). 3 2 Comment 8. However, in the actual device structure discussed in the main text (P(VDF-TrFE)/Fe3GaTe2/P(VDF-TrFE)), Fe3GaTe2 is sandwiched between two PVDF layers, the presence of a rigid substrate does not apply here! The XRD and Raman data shown only characterize the observed phenomena but do not provide a mechanistic explanation for the origin of the asymmetry. This asymmetry is counterintuitive, yet the authors have not provided a satisfactory physical justification, which undermines the publish-ability of the work. 2. Ferroelectric control of magnetic properties is still not convincing. In my original Comment 6, I questioned whether the observed magnetic modulation arises directly from ferroelectric polarization, or instead from the large applied voltages directly affecting Fe3GaTe2. Response 6 does not fully resolve my concern. I do not dispute the intrinsic ferroelectricity of PVDF in this work. And authors have Figure R11 demonstrate the hysteresis loop of this. However, whether the modulation of Fe3GaTe2 magnetism originates from ferroelectric polarization remains unproven. In Figures R8 and supplementary material Figure S7, the hysteresis loops associated with magnetic modulation are weak, continuous, and lack clear abrupt switching. Why don’t they follow the hysteresis loop of PVDF (R11)? This raises the possibility that the results may be indistinguishable from leakage induced “pseudoloops”. The examples authors give on continuous hysteresis loop in BTO, PTO, HZO are about ferroelectricity itself and don’t explain my concern. Such inconclusive evidence does not establish the causal link between ferroelectric switching and magnetic modulation, which is important. .
